Concept

A working venue. A broadcast studio. A stage for what Rock Academy has been building for twenty years.

A live venue, a broadcast and content studio, teaching and rehearsal rooms, and a bar — built as the working home for the next generation of Hudson Valley musicians. Anchored by a twenty-year alumni network. Positioned for a scene that needs it.

Rehearse. Record. Release. Reach an audience. Perform. All from one place. All built for the modern musician.

Kingston–Woodstock Corridor · Location to be selected

01  /  Concept

The idea, in a paragraph.

Thirdspace is a working live venue with a broadcast and content studio attached, a set of teaching and rehearsal rooms, and a bar that ties it all together. It's Rock Academy's second building, with the Woodstock academy staying exactly as it is, and a serious venue in its own right.

The venue hosts weekly live programming, Rock Academy showcases, alumni acts, and touring bookings. The control room doubles as a teaching studio, where students learn engineering, production, and broadcast craft on real work: capturing performances from the live room, producing podcasts, and running streams. Smaller rooms handle lessons, rehearsal, and writing sessions. The bar runs through all of it.

The studio competes on the person at the desk, not the gear. With the right engineer in the chair, the room draws bands that pay to record here and fills the hours the school doesn't need. Around it sits what no other room in the corridor has: teaching, performance, and broadcast in the same building, powered by Rock Academy's twenty-year alumni network. That integration is what makes it different, and what makes it durable.

02  /  Why this, why now

Three reasons it works — and works now.

Why now

The modern musician needs a new kind of room.

The skills required to sustain a music career have shifted fundamentally. Technical craft still matters. So does content, audience, and release strategy. No venue in the Hudson Valley teaches, produces, and platforms all of these under one roof. The gap is real — and widening.

Why here

The corridor is in renaissance — but missing a piece.

Kingston, Woodstock, and the wider corridor have real cultural momentum, political support, and a growing creative economy. BSP's closure left a specific hole. Existing venues serve existing needs. None are designed for young, developing artists at the scale Rock Academy can already deliver.

Why us

Rock Academy is the feeder system.

Twenty-plus years, a large alumni network, political and philanthropic standing, and a team that has earned community trust. No other operator can credibly launch a venue and immediately fill it with talent, audience, families, and story. That is the defensible advantage.

03  /  What we're building

Five interlocking pillars. One venue.

Each pillar is a standalone offering and a revenue stream. Together, they compound: students become performers, performers become content, content draws audiences, audiences fill the bar, the bar funds more programming. The whole is designed to feed itself.

i
The live venue.
Home to the academy's fifteen themed show nights a year, sized to seat every kid's ticket block. Around that, alumni acts, local and touring bookings, and a weekly calendar that gives the venue its rhythm and the community a reason to come back. Competing for audiences and attention on its own merits.
ii
The broadcast studio.
A control room and live room that capture every performance in the building, produce podcasts, run streams, and record sessions. A studio that competes on the engineer, not the console, and doubles as a live classroom. Streams first; a Tiny Desk-style session series once the room exists and visiting artists have somewhere to play.
iii
Teaching & studio craft.
Rock Academy's core teaching extended into the room, and taught the way the academy teaches everything: together. Tracking, mixing, production, lighting, and broadcast run as crew sessions with rotating roles, never as solo screen time. Students then take on supported roles as the venue's trained crew. Modern musicianship too: rights, release strategy, content, audience building. Students own what they make here; the academy holds a license to use it for promotion.
iv
Rehearsal & smaller rooms.
Divisible space for rehearsal, writing sessions, podcast recording, and small-group work. Bands rehearsing in parallel for the first time, which means more shows and more kids per season without touching Woodstock. Hourly rooms and lockouts for local bands in the dark hours. Priority access for Rock Academy members and alumni; layout shaped by what programming actually needs.
v
Bar & hospitality.
Not an afterthought. A proper bar operation that serves the venue, the performances, and the community, and a core revenue line. Kids' nights run as they do today at booked venues with bars: monitored, and not a blocker. The hospitality layer that turns a music space into a place people want to be on a Tuesday night.
Ground rules · agreed 15 September 2026

Rock Academy stays in Woodstock. Thirdspace is an added building, not a move. Students own everything they make here; the academy holds a promotional license and nothing more. Craft is taught together, never alone. The bar is part of the room. Best of Season moves in only if the room is big enough. And nothing in this building changes what the academy is: kids aged 8 to 18, of every ability, sharing one stage.

04  /  Where it sits

A serious venue, with something the others don't have.

The Hudson Valley music scene is served by established venues. What it isn't served by is a single place that integrates teaching, rehearsal, recording, performance, and content production for developing artists — with a ready-made alumni and community feeder system already attached. That integration is what Thirdspace offers, and it is the foundation of the venture.

But a development platform needs a stage — one with the programming, the audience, and the presence to stand on its own. Thirdspace is built to compete — for audiences, for bookings, for attention — as a serious venue in its own right. The development engine runs underneath. The venue runs out front. The same building serves both. And it is designed as a package: the building, the programs inside it, the content model, and the operating plan, so that the next academy comes with a venue attached.

Positioning

A place to rehearse, record, perform, release, and learn the craft of being a working musician — anchored by Rock Academy, open to the wider community.

05  /  What's open

The questions worth working through together.

This concept is deliberately not complete. It describes what Thirdspace is and why it should exist, but leaves several structural questions open — because they are better resolved in partnership than assumed in isolation. These are the conversations this document is intended to open.

01 · Venue

The right home.

Lease, build, or buy. The venues discussed so far sit in the $1m to $2m range. The former BSP Kingston in the Uptown Stockade District remains a strong candidate: approved sound stage, heritage venue bones, known audience, a community-restoration story. A second Kingston listing is on the market and worth a visit with the model in hand. Room size is the first question: it has to seat a themed show's ticket blocks, and it decides whether Best of Season moves in.

02 · Structure

The right entity.

Hybrid for-profit / nonprofit is a working direction, supporting tax advantages, grant eligibility, and protecting the Rock Academy brand. Legal discovery needed to confirm the exact shape.

03 · Capital

The right round.

Investor money is available. The shape of the round follows the NDA now in circulation. Pathways still on the table: Rock Academy founding circle, Thirdspace venture equity, and tax-advantaged educational structures. Quantum and investor mix to be defined against the model.

04 · Team

The right roles.

Existing Rock Academy leadership carries the creative and teaching weight and is already at capacity, so the building needs its own dedicated lead. Jason bridges any replication; his successor at the academy will be a salaried hire. Esther Downton joins on brand and business strategy. Brook Downton owns the business and financial model, broadcast, and capture. The engineer at the desk is an early, deliberate hire. Operations, programming, and front-of-house still to be defined and filled well.

05 · Partnerships

The right allies.

Local political support (Hinchey, Ryan, Figueroa, Delgado) is real. Programming, booking, and national-scale partnerships to be cultivated deliberately.

06 · Model

The right economics.

Five revenue pillars and a Rock Academy feeder system change the financial picture substantially from a standalone venue. The next deliverable, owned by Brook and Esther: a model where building size, price or rent, room count, cohort size, and program mix are sliders, with Woodstock held constant, built for the investor conversation and the location decision.

07 · Replication

The right template.

Connecticut next, with Jason as the bridge, and every replicated academy with a venue attached. Thirdspace is the first of a kind, so what gets designed here is the package. Further cities and other structures have been mentioned, not decided.

06  /  Closing

The bones are here. The trust is here. The gap in the market is here. What's left is to build it well.

Updated after the 15 September 2026 working session.
